analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with high-risk pools, malpractice damage caps, and expanded health savings accounts.
analysis.headline: A repeal-and-replace bill by Rep. Sean Duffy (R-WI) with one cosponsor was sent to three subcommittees and never received a markup, a vote, or a floor debate before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act entirely — its premium subsidies, Medicaid expansion, insurance rules, and tax increases — and put a smaller framework in its place: state high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, malpractice damage caps, permission to sell insurance nationwide under one chosen state's rules, and wider use of health savings accounts. It also raises penalties for Medicare fraud and lets small businesses pool together into association health plans. It was introduced on December 15, 2011 and never moved past subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain from the repeal of the ACA's tax increases. Medical device makers gain from the repeal of the reconciliation act that created the 2.3% device excise tax. Doctors, malpractice insurers, and drug and device makers gain from caps on malpractice damages and a bar on punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products. Insurers gain flexibility from the removal of the individual mandate, guaranteed-issue requirements, and rate rules, and from selling policies under one state's laws nationwide. Small trade associations gain new ability to sponsor association health plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, device makers, doctors, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Expands health savings account eligibility to Medicare Part A beneficiaries, veterans with service-connected disabilities, Indian Health Service patients, and people eligible for TRICARE plans, and gives HSAs the same bankruptcy protection as retirement accounts.
Lets small businesses band together through trade or professional associations into association health plans certified under ERISA, pooling their buying power.
Increases civil money penalties, criminal fines, and prison sentences for Medicare fraud and abuse, and tightens Medicare secondary-payer enforcement in liability cases.
Keeps a ban on annual and lifetime dollar limits on coverage and adds protection against unjust cancellation of policies.
Authorizes HHS awards to states that reduce premiums in the small-group or individual market or reduce the share of uninsured non-elderly residents.
Caps malpractice attorney contingent fees, shortens the window for filing suits, and allows periodic payment of future damage awards, reducing malpractice exposure and premiums for providers.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions would lose the guaranteed-coverage guarantee in the individual market and rely on state high-risk pools, which historically charged high premiums and capped coverage. Low- and middle-income households would lose ACA premium subsidies and the Medicaid expansion. Seniors would lose the closing of the Medicare Part D coverage gap, part of which brand-name drug makers paid. Patients injured by medical care would face a $250,000 cap on non-economic damages, restricted punitive damages, and a bar on punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products. Young adults up to age 25 would lose dependent coverage, which the bill cuts from age 26 to 23. People buying individual policies sold across state lines would have only the chosen 'primary state's' consumer protections.

drawbacks.text: Removes the ACA's prohibition on preexisting-condition exclusions in the individual market, leaving people with health conditions dependent on state high-risk pools or reinsurance programs the bill requires each state to run.

Caps non-economic malpractice damages at $250,000 regardless of the number of defendants, makes punitive damages available only on clear and convincing proof of malicious intent, and bars punitive damages against manufacturers of FDA-approved medical products.

Lets an insurer designate one 'primary state' whose laws govern the individual policies it sells in every other state, freeing those policies from the coverage mandates, rate rules, and consumer protections of the states where the buyers live; the bill's own required notice tells buyers the policy 'may be less expensive' because it is 'not subject to all of the consumer protection laws' of their state.
Repeals the ACA's premium subsidies and Medicaid expansion while cutting dependent coverage from age 26 to 23, shrinking coverage for low-income households and young adults.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs some genuine consumer provisions — no annual or lifetime coverage caps, broader HSA access, tougher Medicare fraud penalties — with a wholesale repeal of the ACA's coverage expansion. The replacement protections are far narrower than what repeal removes: high-risk pools instead of guaranteed coverage, a $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering awards, and the option to sell policies stripped of state consumer protections nationwide. The most substantial gains flow to high-income households, medical device makers, and providers through tax repeal and tort caps, while the largest costs fall on people with preexisting conditions, subsidy recipients, and malpractice victims.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees the day it was introduced, sent to three subcommittees over the next three months, and sat there without a markup, a vote, or a floor debate until the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Sean Duffy (R-WI) introduced the bill on December 15, 2011.

It was referred the same day to eight committees, led by Energy and Commerce, and over the following three months was referred to three subcommittees: Health (Energy and Commerce), Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, and Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions (Education and the Workforce).
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the Affordable Care Act, its subsidies, its insurance rules, and its tax provisions all remained in force, so no industry or household gained anything from this bill's death. The narrow effect of its failure was to preserve the ACA framework that the bill would have dismantled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The ACA stayed law; status quo held

for.name: Rep. Sean Duffy (R-WI)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the repeal-and-replace bill on December 15, 2011.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair Fred Upton, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill the day it was introduced and referred it to its Health Subcommittee; never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill never left the subcommittee.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed House Republican ACA repeal legislation throughout 2011-2012 and would have vetoed a repeal bill; none reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill received no action beyond subcommittee referral in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Repealing the reconciliation act (HCERA) wipes out the 2.3% excise tax on medical devices that helped finance coverage expansion, shifting that cost back to taxpayers or coverage generally. Their gain comes from removing a public revenue source.

The bill caps pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000, restricts punitive damages, limits attorney fees, and shortens filing deadlines, cutting malpractice exposure and premiums. The gain comes directly out of the compensation available to injured patients.

The bill shields makers of FDA-approved products from punitive damages, and ACA repeal would end the brand-name industry's 50% share of the Medicare Part D coverage-gap discount. Both changes raise drug makers' protection while reducing benefits or remedies available to patients.

Repeal removes the individual mandate and ACA subsidies, shrinking the subsidized customer pool, but also removes guaranteed-issue and rate regulation and allows selling individual policies nationwide under one chosen state's laws. The provisions that favor insurers do so by stripping state consumer protections from buyers.
Full ACA repeal eliminates the law's tax increases, including the 3.8% surtax on investment income, with the benefit concentrated among the wealthiest households.

The bill lets trade and professional associations sponsor ERISA-certified association health plans, letting small employers pool buying power. These plans are exempt from many state coverage mandates, so the savings can come from thinner benefit packages.

The malpractice title caps contingent fees on a sliding scale and caps damages, directly reducing plaintiffs' bar income. Their loss mirrors the loss in recoverable compensation for injured patients, so their interest runs alongside patients here.
